vignette:
Captain Liko Tiatia is a 39-year-old Samoan man who has worked as a commercial airline pilot for eight years. In the cockpit, he is a master of precision. The checklists are rituals. The horizon is an absolute. He describes flying as the only place he ever felt truly safe. On the ground, he is a man who has been bracing against a blow for seventeen years.

The trauma happened when he was twenty-two. He was driving home from a night security shift when a police car lit up behind him for a broken taillight. He remembers the cold of the concrete against his cheek, the smell of the asphalt, and the calm voice of the officer who asked if he wanted to die while a knee pressed into his lower back. He was beaten, arrested, and charged with resisting. The charges were dropped. The memory of his own helplessness was not. He quit his job, moved cities, and poured himself into the rigid order of aviation. The sky had no roads, no traffic stops, no badges.

The marriage to Ana worked for a while. She was attracted to his discipline, his quiet strength. But the quiet became distance. The discipline became rigidity. He couldn't explain why he flinched when she touched his neck, or why he would not drive past the police station. He stopped attending church, stopped joining family gatherings. Fa’a Samoa—the Samoan way of family, service, and belonging—felt like a duty he could no longer fulfill. He was a ghost at his own children’s birthdays. “You don’t love us,” Ana said four years ago. “You just survive us.” The divorce was final six months later. He has not been in a relationship since.

Now, the structure he built is collapsing. The sound of the landing gear locking into place is the exact sound of a baton sliding from a ring. The burst of static from air traffic control is the crackle of the cruiser’s radio. When he taxis to the gate and sees the airport police on the perimeter, his heart rate spikes so violently he has to grip the yoke until his knuckles whiten. He has not flown into the city where he was arrested in eleven years. He requested a permanent schedule change to avoid it.

The symptoms are relentless. He has vivid nightmares of being pulled from the flight deck by men in uniform while passengers watch. He wakes in his hotel room on layovers with his fists clenched, the sheet twisted around his legs. He scans every parking lot for patrol cars. He cannot attend his son’s rugby games because the uniformed security at the field triggers a dissociative spell. He snapped at his First Officer last week for a minor deviation in altitude, and the First Officer quietly asked if he was okay. Liko told him he was fine. He was not fine.

His sleep is fractured. He drinks heavily in foreign hotel rooms to blunt the hypervigilance and then lies awake anyway, listening for the knock on the door. He avoids the news. He avoids intimacy. He avoids his own family. The only emotion he feels reliably is a low, grinding anger at the authority he used to trust.

He came to therapy because his medical certification is due for renewal in six weeks. He knows he cannot lie on the psychological evaluation. He sits on the edge of the chair, uniform pressed, posture rigid, eyes fixed on the window. “If I lose my license,” he says quietly, “I lose the only thing that makes sense.” He pauses. “But I don’t know how much longer I can carry the weight of the sky.”
